title: Designing for Observability
summary: Building instrumentation, health checks, and golden signals into a design from day one — because bolting them on after the first incident always costs more.

slides.markdown:
Most teams add observability the same way: after an incident where nobody could tell what was wrong. Designing it in from day one — instead of retrofitting it under pressure — is cheaper and catches problems the retrofit never will, because you instrument based on how the system is supposed to fail, not just how it already has.

This topic covers health checks, golden signals, and the specific interview mistake of drawing a beautiful architecture with zero observability in it.

slides.sectionTitle: Designing observability in, not bolting it on after an incident
slides.markdown:
Instrumentation added *after* an incident is reactive by nature — it answers the specific question that incident raised, but not the next one. A service that had no latency breakdown by endpoint only gets one added for the endpoint that just broke, leaving every other endpoint just as blind as before.

Designing observability in means deciding, while sketching the architecture, what you'd need to know if each component failed — before it has. Concretely: every new service gets a health endpoint, key metrics, and a place in the tracing setup on day one, as part of the definition of "done," not as a follow-up ticket filed after the first outage exposes the gap.

A **liveness check** answers "is this process still running and not deadlocked?" — failing it usually means the orchestrator should restart the instance. A **readiness check** answers a different question: "is this instance ready to receive traffic right now?" — an instance can be alive but not ready, for example while it's still warming a cache or waiting for a database connection on startup.

Conflating the two is a real production bug: if a load balancer routes traffic based on liveness alone, a starting-up instance that's alive-but-not-ready gets real requests it can't yet serve correctly, causing errors that a proper readiness check would have prevented by simply holding traffic back for a few more seconds.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: where instrumentation hooks sit in a request's path
slides.markdown:
![Instrumentation hooks placed at each stage of a request path](assets/instrumentation-points.svg)

Instrumentation isn't one thing bolted on at the edge — it's a set of small hooks placed at each boundary a request crosses: where it enters (gateway metrics and trace start), where a component might not yet be ready (health checks), and where slow dependencies hide (per-call latency at the database boundary). Placing these while designing the request path is far cheaper than retrofitting them after the fact, hop by hop.

slides.sectionTitle: What to instrument on day one: golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation)
slides.markdown:
The **golden signals** are the minimum instrumentation set worth having before anything else: **latency** (how long requests take, and specifically whether failed requests are excluded or skew the number), **traffic** (how much demand the system is under), **errors** (rate of failed requests), and **saturation** (how full the system's most constrained resource is — CPU, memory, connection pool, queue depth).

These four cover most of what "is this service healthy" needs without requiring you to first anticipate every specific failure mode. A new service with these four instrumented from day one is meaningfully more debuggable than one with elaborate custom metrics but none of the basics.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: minimal-viable observability vs everything instrumented from day one
slides.markdown:
| | Minimal-viable (golden signals only) | Everything instrumented from day one |
|---|---|---|
| Setup cost | Low — four metrics, one health endpoint | High — custom metrics, extensive tracing, dashboards for everything |
| Time to ship | Fast | Slower, more upfront design work |
| Debugging a novel failure | Covers most cases; may need to add specific instrumentation reactively | Better coverage, but much of it may go unused |
| Risk | Missing a specific signal for a rare failure mode | Wasted effort building instrumentation nobody queries |

**How to decide:** default to golden signals plus a health endpoint for anything new — that's the floor, not optional. Add deeper, custom instrumentation incrementally as the service's actual failure modes reveal themselves, rather than guessing everything up front.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: an architecture diagram in the interview with zero observability drawn in
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll draw the architecture first and mention monitoring at the end if there's time."

**Why it's wrong:** treating observability as an optional add-on at the end of the conversation signals it was never actually part of the design thinking — and interviewers notice. A beautiful diagram of services, queues, and databases with nothing showing how you'd know any of it is healthy reads as production-inexperienced, regardless of how correct the architecture otherwise is.

**Correct model:** name the golden signals and a health-check strategy for the core services *as you draw them*, the same way you'd name a database choice or a caching layer — observability is a first-class design decision, not a footnote.

slides.sectionTitle: Auto-instrumentation vs manual: how much of the golden-signals floor you get for free
slides.markdown:
Modern instrumentation frameworks (OpenTelemetry's auto-instrumentation agents, for example) can hook into common frameworks and libraries — an HTTP server, a database driver, a queue client — and emit request latency, error rate, and trace spans with no application code changes at all, just a library or agent added at deploy time. This gets a new service most of the golden-signals floor essentially for free on day one.

What auto-instrumentation can't see is business-specific meaning: it knows an HTTP request took 340ms and returned a 500, but not that this particular request was a checkout attempt for a high-value cart, which is exactly the context a manual, custom span or metric would add. The practical pattern most teams land on: auto-instrumentation for the generic golden-signals floor, layered with a small number of hand-written, business-meaningful metrics and spans for the handful of flows that actually matter most.

This is why "instrument on day one" doesn't have to mean writing hundreds of lines of metrics code before the first deploy — the framework-level floor is often a configuration decision, not an engineering one.

slides.sectionTitle: Dashboards-as-code: shipping a starter dashboard in the same PR as the service
slides.markdown:
A service that ships with golden-signals metrics but no dashboard still leaves the first on-call engineer building one from scratch during an actual incident — exactly the wrong moment to be discovering which metric names exist and what a healthy baseline looks like. **Dashboards-as-code** treats the dashboard definition itself (a Grafana JSON model, a Terraform resource, whatever the observability stack uses) as a file checked into the same repository as the service, reviewed in the same pull request that adds the instrumentation.

This does two things a manually-clicked-together dashboard doesn't: it forces the dashboard to exist *before* the service ships, since it's part of the same change, and it keeps the dashboard in sync as metrics are renamed or added, since a stale dashboard referencing a removed metric shows up as a visible diff in review rather than a silently broken panel discovered later.

The net effect is that "can I see this service's health" is answered the moment it deploys, not the first time someone needs it under pressure — the same principle as designing the golden signals in from day one, extended one step further to how a human actually looks at them.
